So... you're planning on Moving all of your clutter?

I've never understood this (though see it frequently), people who box up stuff, arrive at a new place and some boxes remain untouched for years.

Do it now, while you're packing. It's MUCH easier to move less stuff (and cheaper if you're paying someone else). The litmus is, if you haven't touched it, looked at it (for art/collectables), worn it or used it in the last Year, pitch it. My ONE exception is my $$$ formal wear (suits, wifes fancy dresses/jewelry). We may not wear it yearly, but we bought timeless quality items so it'd be available when needed. It all fits in a small armoire that's part of our 1930's Art Deco bedroom suite.

I say this as someone who moved Frequently for the military. It is much nicer to NOT move stuff that just sits around without place or purpose. On a side note, if you think you'll "start over" somewhere different and things will be different somehow, think again. Unless you go through the massive effort of personal change, which is FAR harder than decluttering, your life will fall into the same rut it's in now. I used to think a new place would fix XYZ issue/complaint, but it never did and often just added a new one.

Detailed Review

I don't want to spoil too much about this show because I enjoyed it so much, so I will be intentionally ambiguous!

The show focuses on the research undertaken by Robert Schneck after he heard a campfire story about the "Bye Bye Man": a story of an albino mass murderer and his "sack of gore" who seeks out and murders people who are conscious of his horrific crimes.

Robert Schneck's research led him to the living victims of this story, his publication of the story and the production of the 2017 cinematic release of the film "The Bye Bye Man", in which Schneck shares his experiences and opinions.

This episode was awesome because the "campfire story" is fun if you're prepared to suspend disbelief... and if you are not then Schneck's experiences with researching the story and tracking down the real life victims and being a link in the chain of birthing a Hollywood film is fascinating. Schneck's experience in the creation of a new urban legend and the Hollywood film making process is just fun too.

I'm a huge skeptic of the supernatural and I thoroughly enjoyed ever aspect of this episode and was compelled to (almost) award it full marks for being thoroughly entertaining!

I enjoyed this episode so much that I wanted to keep the review brief and ambiguous and to encourage anyone who is remotely interested to not miss out!

Yeah, I miss Art Bell too, here is his latest cat by the way... but with every recent Heather Wade episode that I've heard, I'm enjoying the show more and more and am legitimately more excited!

Edit: if you are wondering why my reviews are mostly positive, I do skip episodes that I didn't like and focus on the ones which I loved. That said, I have enjoyed almost everything from MITD of late! :-)
